entry.title: A five-field crontab line is not Quartz or EventBridge
entry.summary:
A five-field crontab line is not Quartz and not EventBridge. The every-five-minutes line on classic cron is still */5 * * * *. Build the five fields in the cron expression generator. The page does not install the job. Copy the line onto the host that runs Vixie cron or cronie. Do not add a seconds field on the front of a crontab line. The five fields would shift one place to the right. Quartz uses six fields, or seven when a year is included, and the first field is seconds. Spring cron uses that six-field form. EventBridge also uses six fields, but they are minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, and year, with no seconds field. Quartz and EventBridge both use ? in one of the day fields. A five-field line from this site matches neither shape. */5 * * * *
That line is minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. There is no seconds field. The daemon starts once when the matching minute begins. systemd timers use OnCalendar, which is a different language. Do not paste */5 * * * * into a timer unit. Confirm the expression you want with systemd-analyze calendar on that machine. Call the program by its absolute path when you install the job. Cron's PATH is often shorter than a login shell. Guide: https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-every-5-minutes

Playwright now ships AI test agents: a planner that explores your app and writes a test plan, a generator that turns the plan into tests, and a healer that fixes them when they break. It is one of the most useful things to happen to test automation in years. But a lot of teams run Selenium: Python, Java or C# suites, Selenium Grid, years of tests that work. entry.title: Shipping an LLM feature to production: a 6-step checklist from real client projects
entry.summary: Most LLM prototypes look great in a demo and fall apart the first week real users touch them. Over the last two years our team has taken a number of these prototypes into production for clients in logistics, healthcare and retail. The failures were rarely about the model. They were about everything around it. Here is the checklist we now run before any LLM feature ships. Write 30-50 real example inputs with the answer a domain expert would accept. This becomes your evaluation set. Without it, every prompt change is a guess. For most business use cases, the answer is already in the company's documents. A clean chunking strategy, metadata filters and a re-ranking step usually improve accuracy more than switching to a larger model. Measure retrieval hit-rate separately from answer quality. We build orchestration in ordinary Python modules with typed inputs and outputs rather than deeply nested framework chains. Each step (retrieve, build context, generate, validate) can be unit-tested and swapped. Good Python development practices such as typing, dependency injection and pytest fixtures matter more here than any LLM library. Use structured outputs (JSON schemas) and reject anything that fails validation. For high-risk actions like refunds or record updates, keep a human approval step. Log tokens, latency and cache hit-rate per request. Simple caching of repeated questions and routing easy queries to a smaller model often cut costs by more than half. Documents change, users ask new things, and model versions get updated. Re-run your evaluation set on every release and alert on regressions. Production LLM work is mostly software engineering: evaluation, data quality, testing and monitoring. Teams that treat it that way ship faster and with fewer surprises. That's how we approach AI software development at Mpiric Software. If you're moving a prototype toward production, run through this checklist first.
